title_ar: برنامج مفاهيم في نظر المحامي الأستاذ سلطان بن عبد الله الرشيد
title_en: The Programme "Mafāhīm" in the View of the Lawyer Sultan ibn Abdullah al-Rashid
body_ar: الإمام الموقظ العلامة الددو ( من وحي برنامج مفاهيم والذي عرض على قناة فور شباب ): بُوركت تلك الأنفاس الطاهرة ، و الآراء الباهرة ، صَدَعْتَ بما تدين ، وجَهَرْتَ بما يزين ، بلسان عربي مبين ، فأطلقت للحرية باباً ، و هدمت للتقليد حجاباً ، فانسابت ترفل بين يديك آراء ما ألفتها الأسماع ، و لا اعتادتها الطباع ، حاربت بفعلك آفة الجمود و التقليد ، و خضوع الأعناق للأقوال لغير دليل سديد ، ولا دليل لقائله إلا التقليد ، و ما أدراك ما التقليد ؟ من اعتاده قُيِّد ، وحرم نفسه حرية العقل ، و رحابة الفكر ، و تدبر القرآن ، و تأمل النصوص ، فلا رأي عندك تبديه إلا ما رجح لديك صوابه ، و كُشِفَ عن وجه حسنه لك حجابه ، فلا التقليد قيدك و لا الترهيب أرهبك . و إذا كانت النفوس كباراً تعبت في مرادها الأجسام ، و تقاصرت عن بلوغها الهمم ، و تقازمت دونها القمم ، فسبحان من علم بالقلم . ومن جهر و صدع لا يعلو فوق ندائه همس من خافت وقنع ، و إن كانوا ألف مخافت . لك الله من موقظ منهض ، تجاسر و أقدم حينما تهيب الشجاع و أحجم ، و كنت لها عندما قال الناس من لها : إذا القوم قالوا من فتى خلت أنني عنيت فلم أكسل و لم أتبلد حرك العقول للتفكر ، و شحذ الأذهان للتبصر ، فأسرع الباحثون للتنقيب عن وجه قوله ، و انشغل العالمون بمراجعته في رأيه ، وهذه يقظة ، متى فُقِدَتْ َفقَدَت الأمة نهضتها ، فاليقظة حقائق لا أحلام ، و يقين لا أوهام، و نهوض و تحضر ، و شموخ و تحرر ، و سياحة في الأرض و تبصر ، لا خلود إليها و تسمر ، و نور ساطع مبين ، لا ظلام دامس بهيم . الفوائد في مجالس العلامة غزيرة و الفرائد في مذاكرته وفيرة ، إلا أن أعظمها نفاسة في الميزان وأجلاها نُدرة في الميدان اكتساب شجاعة الصدع بالرأي ، و أنعم بها من شجاعة ، و كلما علا مقام خوف العبد من الله علا مقام شجاعته في بيان دين الله ، قال تعالى " فلا تخشوا الناس و اخشون " وقال جل ذكره " فلا تخافوهم و خافون " فخشية الخالق سبحانه و خوفه تستلزم عدم خشية المخلوق و خوفه ، أي تستلزم الشجاعة ، لذا كان أشدُ الناس خوفاً من الله سبحانه أشجعَهم وهو حبيبنا رسول الله صلى عليه وآله و سلم ، وكما لا يستوي الذين يعلمون و الذين لا يعلمون فكذا لا يستوي الأعمى و البصير و لا الظلمات و لا النور . كتبه: سلطان بن عبدالله الرشيد
body_en:
*[This record is not by Sheikh al-Dedew. It is a tribute addressed to him by a third party, signed at its foot; it is published on his site, and the whole of what follows is that writer's words.]*

The awakening imam, the eminent scholar al-Dedew (written under the inspiration of the programme Mafāhīm, broadcast on the 4Shabab channel):

Blessed be those pure breaths and those dazzling opinions. You spoke out plainly with what you hold as your religion, and proclaimed aloud what adorns, in clear Arabic speech; so you threw open a door to freedom and pulled down a veil that belonged to uncritical following (taqlīd). There flowed forth before you, trailing their robes, opinions that ears had not grown familiar with, nor temperaments grown used to. By what you did you made war on the blight of stagnation and of uncritical following, and on the bowing of necks to sayings that rest on no sound evidence — their speaker having no evidence but uncritical following. And what will make you know what uncritical following is? Whoever grows accustomed to it is shackled, and denies himself freedom of intellect, breadth of thought, reflection upon the Qur'an and contemplation of the texts. You put forward no opinion save one whose correctness has weighed the heavier with you and the veil over whose beauty has been drawn back for you; so uncritical following has not shackled you, nor has intimidation cowed you.

And when souls are great, bodies weary in the pursuit of what those souls desire, aspirations fall short of attaining them, and summits are dwarfed beneath them — so glory be to Him who taught by the pen. One who proclaims aloud and speaks out plainly: no whisper of one who drops his voice and is content rises above his call, though they be a thousand whisperers.

God be with you — an awakener and a rouser, who dared and pressed forward at the moment when the brave man took fright and held back. You were the one for it when people asked, "Who is for it?":

*When the people said, "Who is a young champion?", I supposed that I was the one meant, and so I neither slackened nor played the dullard.*

He set minds moving to reflect and whetted intellects to discern, so that researchers hurried to dig out the grounds of what he said, and the learned busied themselves in taking his opinion up with him. This is wakefulness; whenever it is lost, the community loses its renaissance. For wakefulness is realities and not dreams, certainty and not illusions; it is rising up and becoming civilised, loftiness and liberation, travelling through the earth and discerning — not settling into it and being nailed fast — and a radiant, manifest light, not a deep and unrelieved darkness.

The benefits in the eminent scholar's gatherings are abundant, and the rare gems in his discussion are plentiful; but the most precious of them in the balance, and the plainest of them in its rarity in the field, is the acquiring of the courage to speak out plainly with one's opinion — and how fine a courage that is. The higher the servant's station of fear of God rises, the higher rises his station of courage in expounding God's religion. God Most High said: "So do not fear the people, but fear Me", and He, exalted be His mention, said: "So do not fear them, but fear Me". For awe of the Creator, glory be to Him, and fear of Him entail not standing in awe of the created and not fearing it — that is, they entail courage. Hence the most intensely fearful of God, glory be to Him, was also the most courageous of them: our beloved, the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace. And just as those who know and those who do not know are not equal, so too the blind and the seeing are not equal, nor the darknesses and the light.

Written by: Sultan ibn Abdullah al-Rashid

flags.context: the signature at the foot, against the whole of the body
options: display with a prominent notice that the text is a third party's tribute, not the Sheikh's writing
display among the Sheikh's own texts
flags.note: CRITICAL for display. The entire body is a panegyric addressed TO the Sheikh, in the second person for its first half and the third person thereafter, written by a Saudi lawyer and signed at the foot. It sits in the site's news section under the Sheikh's name. Rendered in English on a page of his corpus without a banner it reads as self-praise published by its subject, which would be damaging and is not what the source does — the Arabic title names the author. The English body therefore opens with an explicit editorial bracket. Do not present this as a text by the Sheikh.

flags.arabic: التقليد ... و ما أدراك ما التقليد ؟ من اعتاده قُيِّد
flags.context: the central charge of the tribute, repeated five times
flags.note: GLOSSARY DIVERGENCE, recorded deliberately. The glossary fixes تقليد as 'following a qualified scholar' and warns against the pejorative 'blind imitation' unless the Arabic is clearly pejorative. Here it unmistakably is: it is paired with 'the blight of stagnation', called a shackle, and contrasted with reasoning from evidence. The neutral glossary rendering would make the passage incoherent. 'Uncritical following' is used as the pejorative sense that stays closest to the glossary's word; 'blind imitation' was rejected as stronger than the Arabic and as carrying a polemical history of its own. A reviewer should confirm the choice, and the glossary may need a second, pejorative entry.

flags.arabic: " فلا تخشوا الناس و اخشون " ... " فلا تخافوهم و خافون "
flags.context: two Qur'anic quotations given with no references
options: render and supply the references in a note
flags.note: The writer quotes two verses with no citation. They are Sūrat al-Māʾidah 5:44 and Sūrat Āl ʿImrān 3:175. The references have been recorded here rather than inserted into the body, because style guide section 4's citation convention applies to the Sheikh's own quotations of scripture and this body is a third party's; inserting them would tidy the source. The closing sentence also alludes, without quoting, to Sūrat al-Zumar 39:9 and Sūrat Fāṭir 35:19–20. Renderings are interpretive.

flags.arabic: إذا القوم قالوا من فتى خلت أنني عنيت فلم أكسل و لم أتبلد
flags.context: a single line of verse embedded in the prose
options: render as prose in italics, per style guide section 4
flags.note: A famous line of early Arabic verse, widely attributed to Amr ibn al-Itnabah, quoted from memory and without attribution, as the Mauritanian register regularly does. Rendered as prose in italics per style guide section 4; no rhymed English attempted. فتى is rendered 'young champion' to carry both the age and the valour the word holds here.

flags.arabic: و إذا كانت النفوس كباراً تعبت في مرادها الأجسام
flags.context: embedded in the prose without quotation marks
options: render as the writer's prose, noting the allusion
flags.note: This is the first hemistich and a half of a celebrated line of al-Mutanabbi, absorbed into the prose with no marking. The source does not present it as a quotation and the English does not either; recorded so that a reviewer can decide whether the corpus marks unattributed classical quotation.

flags.context: the CMS date stamp against the record's own URL slug
flags.note: SOURCE DEFECT. The record's displayed date is 1 January 2011, but its Joomla slug encodes 2012-03-01 09:55:28, and the record sits between items stamped 27 February 2012 and 10 March 2012. The March 2012 date is almost certainly right and the stamp wrong. Both are preserved: the date field follows the displayed stamp, as everywhere in this corpus, and this flag records the conflict. Neither date is evidence of composition in any case — see the note on CMS upload dates.

translator_notes: NOT a text by Sheikh al-Dedew. A signed tribute to him by the lawyer Sultan ibn Abdullah al-Rashid, prompted by the Sheikh's television programme Mafāhīm on the 4Shabab channel. Published in the site's news section.

The Arabic is sustained rhymed prose (sajʿ), rhyming in long stretches. English cannot carry that without distorting the sense, and the style guide forbids rhymed English for verse; the rhyme has therefore been let go and the register kept elevated. A reader of the English is not seeing the feature that is most conspicuous in the Arabic.
The CMS date on this record conflicts with its own URL slug — see the flag. Both are upload metadata, not composition dates.
مفاهيم is left as a transliterated programme name with its meaning, 'Concepts', deliberately not substituted, since the programme is known by its Arabic name.
